column2: (a) A function is one-to-one when distinct allowed inputs have distinct outputs; (b) its graph passes the horizontal-line test.
column3: The implication f(a)=f(b) ⇒ a=b expresses injectivity. A horizontal line y=c marks all inputs with output c, so at most one intersection is permitted.
column4: This is different from the vertical-line test, which only determines whether the curve is a function.

column2: (a) f⁻¹ maps each y∈B to the unique x∈A with f(x)=y; its domain is B and range A. (b) Solve y=f(x) for x, then rename variables. (c) Reflect the graph across y=x.
column3: The inverse reverses ordered pairs (x,y)→(y,x). Uniqueness follows from one-to-one behavior.
column4: An inverse function is not the reciprocal 1/f; the domain/range swap is part of its definition.

column3: The table has f(2)=2.0 and f(6)=2.0 at different inputs.
column4: A single repeated output is enough to disprove injectivity.

column3: The table gives f(2)=1.9=f(6), although 2≠6.

column3: Draw a horizontal line between the graph's lower and upper heights: it crosses both the rising and falling portions.
column4: Those two intersections share one output but have different inputs.

column3: The displayed curve is strictly increasing from left to right, so any horizontal line crosses it at most once.
column4: Strict monotonicity guarantees different outputs for different inputs on this domain.

column3: The curve is strictly decreasing; each output height occurs at most once.
column4: A decreasing function can be one-to-one just as an increasing function can.

column3: The curve turns downward after its local high; a horizontal line just below that high crosses it twice. Lower horizontal levels also can repeat on its left dip.
column4: Failing the horizontal-line test anywhere is sufficient.

column3: If 2a−3=2b−3, then 2a=2b and a=b; equivalently the line has nonzero positive slope.
column4: An affine function with nonzero slope has a unique inverse.
The even fourth-power symmetry creates repeated outputs.

column4: Sine is periodic, so 1−sin x cannot be injective on all real inputs.

column3: If ∛a=∛b, cubing gives a=b. The cube-root graph is strictly increasing on ℝ.
column4: Odd roots preserve the order of real numbers.

column2: Not one-to-one during the full flight.
column3: The football reaches the same height once while rising and again while falling.
column4: It can become one-to-one on a restricted ascent-only or descent-only time interval.

column3: A person's height can stay nearly constant over many ages, and similar heights can occur before and after later-life shrinkage.
column4: A single height does not uniquely identify an age; no strict monotonicity is justified over an entire life.

column3: (a) f(6)=17 reverses to f⁻¹(17)=6. (b) f⁻¹(3)=2 reverses to f(2)=3.
column4: Inverse notation reverses the input-output relationship rather than taking a reciprocal.

column3: For f(x)=x⁵+x³+x, f(1)=3; it is strictly increasing because each odd-power term increases, so this input is unique. The second expression cancels by the inverse identity.
column4: The domain and range of f are ℝ, so 2 lies in the domain of the inverse.

column3: Evaluate g(0)=3+0+e⁰=4. Both x and e^x increase, hence g is strictly increasing and there is no second solution.
column4: Recognizing the required forward value avoids trying to isolate x+e^x symbolically.

column3: The drawn f-curve passes the horizontal-line test. Read its x-extent [−3,3] and y-extent [−1,3] and swap them. At y=2 the curve has x=0; at y=0 it crosses near x=−1.7.
column4: Inverse evaluation reads horizontally to the original curve and then down to its input axis. Graph estimates are approximate.

column3: Starting from C=(5/9)(F−32), multiply by 9/5 and add 32. The given lower bound F≥−459.67 maps to C≥−273.15.

column3: From m=m0/√(1−v²/c²), obtain 1−v²/c²=(m0/m)², then solve for the nonnegative v.
column4: Speed is nonnegative, so choose the positive root. The inverse gives the speed corresponding to relativistic mass in the textbook's historical notation; assume m0>0 and c>0.

column3: Subtract 1 from y=1+√(2+3x), square to get (y−1)²=2+3x, and solve for x.
column4: The original range y≥1 is essential; without it, squaring would admit outputs that the original root cannot produce.

column3: Multiply y=(4x−1)/(2x+3) by its denominator: 2xy+3y=4x−1. Gather x terms: x(2y−4)=−1−3y.
column4: The original function excludes x=−3/2, and its range excludes y=2. The inverse swaps these domain/range restrictions.

column3: Taking ln of y=e^(2x−1) gives ln y=2x−1; solve for x.
column4: The exponential's positive range becomes the inverse's domain.

column3: Complete the square y+1/4=(x−1/2)². The original restriction x≥1/2 selects x−1/2=+√(y+1/4).
column4: The other quadratic root lies on the discarded branch and is not the requested inverse.

column3: From y=ln(x+3), exponentiate to x+3=e^y and subtract 3.
column4: The inverse outputs values greater than −3, matching the original logarithm's domain.

column3: Let q=e^(−x)>0. Then y=(1−q)/(1+q) implies q=(1−y)/(1+y). Taking −ln gives x=ln((1+y)/(1−y)).
column4: Both numerator and denominator of the positive ratio require the original output range (−1,1).

column3: From y=√(4x+3), square and solve for x. Plot the original root from (−3/4,0) and its inverse parabola branch from (0,−3/4), reflected about y=x.
column4: The inverse is restricted to y≥0 as its input; an unrestricted full parabola would not be the inverse graph.

column3: From y=1+e^(−x), subtract 1, take ln, and negate. The original horizontal asymptote y=1 reflects to the inverse's vertical asymptote x=1.
column4: Use swapped points (0,2)↔(2,0) to check the reflection in y=x; both functions decrease.

column2: Reflect the supplied polyline in y=x; its vertices become (−2,−3),(−1,−1),(2,0),(3,1).
column3: Read the original vertices (−3,−2),(−1,−1),(0,2),(1,3), interchange the two coordinates, and connect consecutive reflected points.
column4: The original graph is increasing, so the reflection is a function and gives its inverse.

column2: A decreasing curve reflected across y=x, passing through (0,2) and the reflected intercepts of the original curve.
column3: Every original point (a,b) becomes (b,a). In particular the original zero at x=2 becomes inverse value f⁻¹(0)=2; the original y-intercept becomes an inverse x-intercept.
column4: Preserve the original curve's endpoint inclusion and curvature after reflection. The horizontal-line test ensures this reflected curve is a function.

column2: f⁻¹(x)=√(1−x²) on [0,1], the same function as f; the graph is a quarter-circle.
column3: From y=√(1−x²), square to x²+y²=1. With x,y∈[0,1], solving for x gives the same square-root rule.
column4: The first-quadrant quarter-circle is symmetric about y=x, explaining the self-inverse property.

column3: Cube y=∛(1−x³) to obtain x³+y³=1; solving for x gives ∛(1−y³). The curve is strictly decreasing and symmetric under swapping coordinates.
column4: The domain is all real numbers because cube roots admit negative values; unlike a circle, the curve has unbounded branches.

column2: (a) log_b x=y iff b^y=x, b>0,b≠1; (b) domain (0,∞); (c) range ℝ; (d) for b>1, increasing through (1,0), vertical asymptote x=0.
column3: The logarithm reverses an exponential. Since b^y is positive for every y, only positive inputs can be logged, while every real exponent can occur as an output.
column4: Graph points (b,1),(1,0),(1/b,−1) and reflect the corresponding exponential about y=x.

column2: (a) ln x=log_e x; (b) log x commonly means log₁₀x; (c) ln x and e^x reflect across y=x.
column3: The points (0,1),(1,e),(−1,1/e) on e^x swap to (1,0),(e,1),(1/e,−1) on ln x.
column4: The logarithm has domain x>0 and vertical asymptote x=0; the exponential has horizontal asymptote y=0.

column3: 2⁵=32 gives log₂32=5. Since 8=2³, 8^(1/3)=2, giving log₈2=1/3.
column4: A logarithm asks for the exponent that produces its argument.
Reciprocals of positive powers correspond to negative exponents.

column3: Combine products and quotients: log₁₀40+log₁₀2.5=log₁₀100=2; log₈60−log₈3−log₈5=log₈4=2/3 because 8^(2/3)=4.
column4: The product/quotient rules require the same base, as used here.

column3: e^(−ln2)=e^(ln(1/2))=1/2. For e^(ln(ln3)), cancel e and the outer logarithm, leaving ln3, which is a valid positive inner argument.
column4: In a nested logarithm, identify the complete argument being inverted; do not cancel an extra layer.
An outside multiplier becomes an exponent of the logarithm's argument.

column2: ln(bc²/d³), for the original positive arguments b,c,d.
column3: Use 2ln c=ln c² and 3ln d=ln d³, then combine addition as multiplication and subtraction as division.
column4: Keep the original domain b>0,c>0,d>0 even if the combined logarithm alone would admit extra sign combinations.

column3: The first term is (1/3)ln((x+2)³)=ln(x+2). The second is (1/2)ln x−ln(x²+3x+2). Factor x²+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2) and cancel inside the combined logarithm.
column4: The original ln x forces x>0, making all canceled factors positive and validating the logarithm laws.

column3: Use change of base: log₅10=ln10/ln5 and log₃57=ln57/ln3, then round only the final quotients to six decimal places.
column4: The base determines the denominator logarithm; reversing the quotient gives the reciprocal value.

column2: All pass through (1,0), increase, and tend to −∞ as x→0+. For x>1, log₁.₅x>ln x>log₁₀x>log₅₀x; the order reverses for 0<x<1.
column3: Change base to ln x/ln b. The positive denominators grow with b, so for positive ln x the quotient decreases as the base grows.
column4: For x<1 the numerator is negative, reversing the visual ordering.

column2: ln x mirrors e^x across y=x, and log₁₀x mirrors 10^x. Both exponentials pass through (0,1); both logarithms through (1,0).
column3: Use e^x and ln x as one inverse pair and 10^x and log₁₀x as the other. For x>0, 10^x>e^x; for x>1, ln x>log₁₀x.
column4: A common plotting window can compress the logarithms compared with exponentials; their domains and reflected asymptotes still differ.

column3: Three feet of height is 36 grid units because each unit is one inch. Solve log₂x=36 to get x=2³⁶ inches, then divide by 63360 inches per mile.
column4: Convert the desired physical height to the graph's coordinate unit before exponentiating.

column2: x^0.1 finally surpasses ln x at x≈3.431×10¹⁵, and stays above afterward.
column3: Set u=ln x. Equality becomes e^(u/10)=u; the upper solution is u≈35.77152064, so x=e^u≈3.431×10¹⁵. For larger u, the exponential ultimately outgrows u.
column4: The much smaller first crossing is not the final one. A modest graph window can misleadingly suggest the logarithm always remains larger.

column2: (a) log₁₀(x+5): domain x>−5, asymptote x=−5, zero x=−4. (b) −ln x: domain x>0, asymptote x=0, zero x=1, decreasing.
column3: For (a), shift the common logarithm left five. For (b), reflect ln x across the x-axis.
column4: Logarithmic input translation moves the vertical asymptote; an outside minus leaves the domain unchanged.

column2: (a) ln(−x): domain x<0, zero x=−1, asymptote x=0. (b) ln(abs(x)): domain x≠0, zeros ±1, even.
column3: Reflect ln x about the y-axis for (a). For (b), keep ln x on the positive side and mirror it onto the negative side.
column4: As x approaches zero from either admitted side the logarithmic output tends to −∞.

column2: (a) domain (0,∞), range ℝ; (b) x=e^(−2); (c) increasing ln curve shifted up 2 with asymptote x=0.

column4: A vertical shift does not change the logarithm's input restriction.

column2: (a) domain (1,∞), range ℝ; (b) x=1+e; (c) ln graph shifted right 1 and down 1, asymptote x=1.

column4: The horizontal shift moves the vertical asymptote and the domain boundary together.

column4: Both signs in (a) are allowed because the logarithm's argument equals positive e³ at each solution.

column2: (a) Both equal 300; (b) a limited calculator may overflow while computing e³⁰⁰ before applying ln, although the exact result is still 300.

column3: The radicand x³+x²+x+1=(x+1)(x²+1) gives original domain x≥−1. Its derivative 3x²+2x+1>0, so f is one-to-one with range y≥0. Squaring y=√(x³+x²+x+1), then putting x=u−1/3, gives u³+(2/3)u+20/27−y²=0; apply the real Cardano formula.

column4: Arcsine's domain is [−1,1] and range [−π/2,π/2]; the entire unrestricted sine cannot have a single inverse.

column4: The endpoints are excluded for tangent, and arctangent never reaches its limiting endpoint values.

column4: The principal inverse-trigonometric domain restricts the entire inner expression.
